title: Divya Deshmukh Becomes First Indian Woman to Win FIDE World Cup, Earns Grandmaster Title
excerpt: The 19-year-old from Nagpur defeated veteran Koneru Humpy in an all-Indian final at Batumi, Georgia, capping a breakthrough tournament run
body:
• Divya Deshmukh, 19, won the 2025 FIDE Women's World Cup in Batumi, Georgia, becoming the first Indian woman to claim the title.
  • She defeated veteran GM Koneru Humpy 2½–1½ in an all-Indian final decided by rapid tiebreaks.
  • The victory automatically earned her the Grandmaster title — India's 88th GM and the fourth Indian woman to achieve it — without having collected a single GM norm beforehand.
  • Deshmukh qualifies for the 2026 Women's Candidates Tournament alongside Humpy and former World Champion Tan Zhongyi.

Divya Deshmukh, a 19-year-old International Master from Nagpur, Maharashtra, defeated fellow Indian Koneru Humpy in a tense tiebreaker to win the 2025 FIDE Women's World Cup in Batumi, Georgia, on July 28. She is the first Indian woman to win the tournament and only the third champion in its history, following Russia's Alexandra Kosteniuk (2021) and Aleksandra Goryachkina (2023).

An All-Indian Final for the Ages

The final pitted two generations of Indian chess against each other. Humpy, 38, became India's first woman Grandmaster in 2002 and has been a fixture at the top of women's chess for over two decades. Deshmukh, born nearly two decades later, entered the World Cup seeded lower but tore through a field of 107 players from 46 federations — including 17 of the world's top 20 — to reach the title match.

https://x.com/ChessbaseIndia/status/2089671915833041307

On her path to the final, Deshmukh eliminated China's Zhu Jiner (world No. 6), Indian veteran Harika Dronavalli, and former Women's World Champion Tan Zhongyi of China. Humpy reached the final by outlasting top-seeded Lei Tingjie of China in a grueling semifinal that stretched through rapid, fast-rapid, and blitz tiebreaks.

Both classical games in the final ended in draws, sending the match to a pair of 15+10 rapid tiebreak games.

Tiebreak Drama in Batumi

In the first rapid game, Deshmukh had a winning position after Humpy blundered under time pressure on move 33, but the younger player missed a critical continuation on move 37 that would have sealed the point. The game ended in a draw.

"A big missed chance for Divya."

— Viswanathan Anand, five-time World Champion, commenting on the first tiebreak game

The second game proved decisive. Humpy opened with a Catalan, and Deshmukh chose an aggressive pawn-grab variation. With over 11 minutes on her clock against Humpy's three, the positional balance shifted sharply when Humpy pushed 40.e4 and followed with the blunder 41.d5, handing Deshmukh a winning attack. The game transitioned into a rook endgame where Deshmukh converted her advantage to clinch the title 1.5–0.5 in the tiebreaks, 2½–1½ overall.

From Zero Norms to Grandmaster

Perhaps the most remarkable aspect of Deshmukh's run is what it earned her beyond the trophy. She entered the tournament without a single Grandmaster norm — the performance benchmarks typically required for the title. Under FIDE regulations, winning the Women's World Cup automatically confers the GM title, bypassing the standard three-norm, 2500-rating pathway.

Deshmukh became India's 88th Grandmaster and the fourth Indian woman to hold the title, joining Humpy, Harika Dronavalli, and Vaishali Rameshbabu.

"I still need time to process it. I think it was fate, me getting the Grandmaster title this way, because before this I didn't even have one norm, and now I'm a Grandmaster."

— Divya Deshmukh, after winning the Women's World Cup

The $50,000 first prize adds to a breakthrough 12 months for the Nagpur native. She won the World Junior Championship in the girls' category last year and played a key role in India's gold medal run at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest, where she also earned an individual gold.

India's Chess Machine Keeps Rolling

The all-Indian final underscored India's ascent as the dominant force in global chess. D. Gukesh's victory at the 2024 FIDE World Championship, R. Praggnanandhaa's continued rise, and now Deshmukh's World Cup title paint a clear picture: India is producing elite chess talent at a pace no other country can match.

Both Deshmukh and Humpy have qualified for the 2026 Women's Candidates Tournament, along with third-place finisher Tan Zhongyi. For Deshmukh, that tournament represents the next step — a shot at challenging for the Women's World Championship itself.

"It's hard for me to speak now. Of course, this definitely means a lot, but there is a lot more to achieve, so I am hoping that this is just the start," she said after embracing her mother at the board in Batumi.
